Module 8 · Reviewing theatre, part 3

The Room We're All In Now

Module 7 asked who gets to review, and what shapes the position they speak from. This week, we shift the question outward: where does reviewing happen now, and what does that space do to the judgement itself?

Audio introduction

Three minutes.

Because a review does not simply enter the world unchanged. The platform, format, audience and speed of response all shape what can be said, how it is said, and what happens to it once it starts circulating.

Before you start reading, open a new tab and find three public responses to The Jungle and the Sea. They do not all need to be reviews. In fact, it is better if they come from different parts of the wider conversation around the production. One might be a professional review, while the others could be a star rating, an audience comment, a social post, a short video, a newsletter, a podcast segment, or even a line of marketing copy.

Save the links somewhere easy to find. For now, resist the urge to analyse them or decide which one is the most useful. Ten minutes should be enough.

You'll come back to these examples later.

What this page is for

By the end of this page, you should be able to:

  • explain how digital platforms have changed not just where criticism appears, but how it is produced, circulated and received
  • describe both sides of that shift: digital criticism has opened participation to more people, while platforms also sort, rank and compress what becomes visible
  • identify what a platform tends to reward, such as speed, brevity, engagement, visibility and the performance of credibility, and point to those pressures in a specific example
  • distinguish between different forms of critical response, including a newspaper review, long-form essay, newsletter, short-form video, audience comment, aggregated score and repost
  • recognise that these forms are not simply shorter or longer versions of the same thing, but different kinds of critical activity
  • identify common habits or shortcuts in reviewing, and notice when they are shaping a response
  • ask practical questions of any review or response: Where is it published? Who is it for? How did it reach me? What format does the platform impose? What is the platform encouraging me to do next?

The page is organised into eight sections. It starts with who is speaking and where criticism now happens, then looks briefly at how we got here. From there, we move into the way platforms shape criticism, the different forms reviews can take, and some of the habits reviewers fall into. We then look at what changes when the performance itself is no longer there to return to, before coming back to the Australian context and, finally, to your own position as a reviewer.

Section 1Where criticism happens

Last week you thought about the reviewer: who they are, what they know, what they have seen before, and how all of that shapes the judgement they arrive at. That question has not gone away. But a review is not only the product of the person who wrote it. It is also shaped by wherever it ends up.

Duška Radosavljević describes criticism as a landscape that keeps changing shape, and suggests that the digital version of it is better understood as a cyberscape. A landscape is something you stand outside and survey. A cyberscape is something you are already inside, moving through, and being moved by. When you read a review online, you are not observing the critical conversation from a distance. You are in it, and the way you arrived there is part of what you are reading.

Alison Croggon offers a good starting point for thinking about what changed, partly because she does not begin by mourning the loss of professional authority. She begins by acknowledging what the internet genuinely opened up. Before it, a small number of people decided which responses to theatre became public. Afterwards, conversation became faster, more lateral and much harder to control. The kinds of things people had always said about theatre, in the foyer or on the way home, could now be said in public and read.

What was new was not the existence of this opinion, but its public airing.

Alison Croggon

That shift mattered. A company could hear directly from the people in its seats. A critic could be answered back. People with kinds of knowledge and experience that newspapers had never sought out could join the conversation without waiting for permission.

But Croggon's argument does not stop there. What happened next is that the spaces where this conversation was taking place began to change. Independent blogs were absorbed into larger organisations. Social media became the default setting for online life. And the shape of the internet came to be determined by a handful of very large companies, by search rankings, by advertising, and by the quiet work of making content findable.

So the useful question is not whether more people can now speak. They obviously can. The question is what happens to what they say: where it lands, how far it travels, who encounters it, and what shape it has to take in order to be seen at all.

Section 2A short history of changing criticism

It is easy to talk about the present as though everything has suddenly changed, either for the worse or for the better. But criticism has been reshaped several times before. Each shift changed who could speak, who got paid, how long a review could be, and what counted as public judgement.

Print culture. Reviews took their form from the systems around them: word limits, deadlines, editorial priorities, a known readership and a payment structure. Critics worked within those conditions whether they chose them or not.

Broadcast and mass media. The audience became much larger, but the formats often became shorter. Arts discussion could reach more people, though usually with less space for detail. That trade-off did not begin with social media.

Online reviewing, from the mid-1990s. Andrew Haydon traces the early years of UK online theatre criticism, when many websites still looked a lot like newspapers transferred onto a screen. WhatsOnStage, generally regarded as the first British theatre website, launched in 1996 and published its first review, of Ben Elton's Popcorn, in 1997. Around the same time, Peter Lathan launched British Theatre under the American company that later became About.com. When that company closed hundreds of its sites in 2001, Lathan kept the material and relaunched it independently as British Theatre Guide.

There is a pattern here that will become familiar: critical work often survives by moving on from the platform that first carried it.

What was more unusual at the time was everything that began appearing around the review: user reviews, forums and comment threads. Suddenly, published criticism could be answered publicly and immediately.

A note on stars. The five-star rating reached theatre before today's platforms did, and it emerged for a fairly practical reason. By 1996 the Edinburgh Fringe programme contained around 1,500 shows, and The Scotsman introduced a one-to-five-star scale to help readers navigate them. WhatsOnStage used the same system from its first review.

These were critics' ratings, not audience scores. Audience star ratings arrived much later in British theatre and never became quite as established. Early experiments at the Fringe with customer ratings by text message were easy to manipulate, and when Stagedoor launched in 2017, allowing anyone to rate a production was still treated as something relatively new.

So the impulse to compress judgement into a number did not begin with platform culture. It began as a way of dealing with too much choice. Fifteen hundred shows and one programme already creates a problem that a number solves much faster than a paragraph.

That is worth remembering when we get to platforms in the next section. Digital platforms did not invent the shortcut. They made it much more widespread and much more powerful.

The blogosphere, through the 2000s. Blogs changed the conditions again. Writers no longer needed institutional permission to publish, and Haydon describes something close to a punk spirit around that period: anyone with an internet connection could start writing, and anyone interesting enough could find an audience.

The newspapers noticed. By 2006, The Guardian had begun investing seriously in online publishing and created a series of more informal, comment-friendly blogs, including one devoted to theatre. Within a few years, some of the liveliest conversations about British theatre were happening not only in reviews, but underneath them, in comment threads and on independent blogs written by people traditional newspapers had never employed.

Feeds, from the 2010s. By this point, the main question was no longer simply who could publish. Almost anyone could. The harder question became who could actually be seen: who was shared, surfaced, searched, recommended, and who had the time and resources to keep producing work.

Section 3What platforms do to criticism

There are two things happening at once here, and both matter.

On one hand, digital platforms have opened criticism up. You no longer need a newspaper, an editor or an established cultural network behind you in order to publish. Criticism can be more conversational, more immediate, and sometimes much more inventive. Writers can build their own audiences, and forms that would never fit into a 400-word newspaper review can find a home.

At the same time, those responses are now moving through platforms that sort, rank and measure them. Likes, shares, stars, clicks and recommendation systems all affect what becomes visible. A complicated judgement can be reduced to a number, while criticism competes for attention with marketing, outrage and everything else in the feed.

The important point is that these two developments do not cancel each other out. The same systems that made it easier for more people to speak also shape which voices are heard and how their responses circulate.

And you do not need to be a reviewer for this to affect you. A rating, a click, a share, even the decision to scroll past something all become part of the way a production is encountered online.

There are six pressures worth paying attention to.

Speed. Platforms favour quick responses. The first reaction can become more visible than the one that took longer to think through.

Visibility. What reaches you has already been sorted through search results, rankings, recommendations and popularity signals. What you do not see matters too.

Compression. Stars, scores, percentages and thumbs turn a complicated response into something that can be read at a glance, compared and averaged.

Engagement. A response that makes people react is likely to travel further. But provoking a reaction and helping someone understand a work are not necessarily the same thing.

Credibility. Reviewers often have to establish very quickly why you should listen to them. They may point to how often they attend theatre, their professional experience, their access, or their identity. Notice how early this kind of positioning appears.

Governance. Platforms also decide what remains visible, what is moderated, what disappears and what is promoted. Those decisions shape cultural conversation, even though they are usually made far away from the people having it.

Tom Vanderbilt, writing about sites such as Yelp, Amazon and IMDb rather than theatre, describes one consequence of all this. When there are hundreds or thousands of responses to choose from, you start judging not only the thing being reviewed, but the person reviewing it: their taste, expertise, expectations and credibility.

I find myself reviewing the reviewers.

Tom Vanderbilt

Of course, that part is not entirely new. Audiences have always trusted some critics more than others. What has changed is the scale. You might now be looking at hundreds of people with different standards, different expectations and very little context for understanding where any of them are coming from. That can be liberating, but it can also make judgement harder rather than easier.

Cher Tan's discussion of the Facebook news blackout in Australia shows another side of platform power. When Facebook stopped distributing news, its systems also caught literary journals, emergency services, health information and satire. The point is bigger than that particular incident. Platforms do not simply carry cultural conversation. They make decisions about what becomes visible and reachable in the first place.

One piece of content is the same as any other piece of content as long as it gets you the eyeballs you need.

Tim Hwang, quoted in Cher Tan

Activity

Go back to one of the three responses you collected, preferably one you would normally skim past. Which of these pressures can you see shaping it? You will probably find more than one.

Section 4Different forms of reviewing

You already know most of these forms because you encounter them all the time. What is useful here is to start noticing what each one allows a reviewer to do, and what becomes harder to do within it. A newspaper review, an audience comment and a TikTok response are not simply longer or shorter versions of the same thing. They create quite different relationships between the production, the person responding to it, and the people reading or watching.

The newspaper or magazine review. A critic is usually writing to a deadline, for a broad readership, and within a fairly tight word count. They need to describe the production, make an argument about it and give readers enough context to understand that argument, often in only a few hundred words.

That takes considerable skill, but something will inevitably be left out. A production that needs cultural, historical or dramaturgical context may be particularly difficult to account for in 500 words.

Go and look. Find a professional review of The Jungle and the Sea. Notice how much space the reviewer gives to explaining the Sri Lankan civil war before moving into judgement, and what has had to be left out to make room for it.

The blog or long-form essay. Here, the writer usually has more room. They can follow an idea further, write personally, bring in theory, or spend much longer with one aspect of a production. Haydon argues that this expansion of forms genuinely changed what could be written and understood about theatre. The difficulty is keeping it going. Much of this writing is unpaid, and many independent blogs disappear when their writers can no longer sustain the work.

Go and look. Independent Melbourne theatre blogs cover far more of the city's work than the newspapers do. Find a review of any production on one of them, and compare its length and its interests with a newspaper review of the same show.

The newsletter. A newsletter creates a smaller and often more direct relationship between writer and reader. It can bypass some of the traditional gatekeeping of newspapers and magazines, but it brings other demands. The writer has to build an audience, keep people subscribed and produce work regularly. Independence does not necessarily mean freedom from pressure.

The short-form video review. Here, the reviewer's voice, face, timing and personality become part of the response. That can make criticism immediate, accessible and much closer to the way people actually talk about something they have just seen. But the format also favours a strong opening, speed and a clear position. There is often less room to hesitate, qualify a judgement or spend time describing why something produced a particular response.

Go and look. Search the production's title on TikTok or Instagram. Watch the first few seconds closely. What does the reviewer need to do to keep you watching, and how does that shape everything that follows?

The audience comment. Audience comments can tell us something very directly about how a performance landed with the people who saw it. They can capture emotional and social responses that a professional review might miss. But there is an important difference between saying "I hated this" and identifying what happened in the production that produced that response. Look for the moment when preference becomes observation.

Go and look. Comments under a theatre company's own social media posts, or replies to a published review, are the easiest place to find these. Look for one comment that does move from preference into observation, and one that does not.

★★★★☆

The aggregated star score. A score is useful because it is quick. That is also its problem. An average can tell you that a group of people responded positively or negatively, but it cannot tell you why. Disagreement, context and reasoning disappear into the number. Croggon is particularly critical of this model because it places a theatre production into the same consumer-rating system we use for restaurants, hotels and products.

Go and look. Compare the star rating at the top of a review with what the review actually says. Does the number hold up against the reasoning underneath it? You will often find a four-star review with serious reservations in its final paragraph.

The repost or quote-post. Sharing someone else's response is also a form of participation. A person can repost a review to endorse it, challenge it, mock it or direct other people towards it. The original response therefore gains another layer of meaning as it circulates.

When this happens at scale, the response to a review can sometimes become more visible than the review itself.

Section 5Critical habits

Susan Best, writing about Australian art criticism, identifies three habits that critics can easily slip into. They are not fixed types of people, and they are not signs that someone is a "bad" critic. They are simply tendencies worth noticing in your own writing.

The curmudgeon keeps a strong distance from the work. That distance can help with judgement, but it can also harden into a kind of certainty where curiosity disappears.

The insider knows the field well: the artists, the history, the references, the conventions. That knowledge can be incredibly useful, but it can also make everything feel familiar. When nothing feels strange anymore, it becomes harder to notice what is actually happening in front of you.

The press-release summariser gets the facts right and describes the production carefully, but stops before making a judgement. The writing may be accurate, yet still leave the reader unsure what the critic actually thinks.

Best offers another image for criticism: the critic as a window cleaner. The critic is not standing above the work delivering a final verdict, and they are not simply repeating the language a company has already used to describe itself. Their job is to make something easier to see, to help a reader notice what was pleasurable, difficult, confusing, surprising or unresolved in the encounter.

Jane Howard adds another complication, particularly in the Australian context. Criticism depends on conversation, but conversation can be difficult to sustain in a relatively small arts community. In Melbourne, the critic, artist, publicist, venue and funding body may all be only a few connections apart. That closeness can create care and attentiveness, but it can also make disagreement feel more personal. Sometimes that produces caution. Sometimes defensiveness. Sometimes people simply decide not to say anything at all.

Section 6What remains after the performance

Online platforms often place theatre alongside books, films, restaurants and hotels, but theatre is different in one important way: the thing being reviewed no longer exists in exactly the same form once the performance is over.

A production happens at a particular time, in a particular place, with a particular audience. Afterwards, what remains are records of that event: reviews, production photographs, trailers, interviews, audience posts, podcasts, archival recordings, marketing material and people's memories.

Digital media have made these records easier to preserve and circulate, but they are still not the performance itself. A trailer may remain online for years, but it only shows selected moments. A social post may capture an immediate reaction, but not the full experience of watching the work. An archival recording can preserve staging and performance, but watching it on a screen is not the same as being in the theatre.

This is why Diana Damian Martin's argument is useful: the internet should be understood as a context for criticism, not as something that automatically makes criticism better or worse. Digital responses are shaped by the medium in which they appear.

The Jungle and the Sea gives us a useful case to think with because the play itself is concerned with memory, loss, testimony and what survives after an event. Once the production closes, our understanding of it will also depend on what has been recorded and remembered.

Activity

So when you look at a digital response to the production, ask: what kind of record is this? Is it criticism, documentation, promotion, memory, recommendation, or a mixture of several of these?

Section 7Reviewing in Australia

A lot of the history of digital criticism is told through London or New York, but reviewing in Australia has developed under quite different conditions. Theatre here is spread across cities that are a long way apart, while most productions remain local. A critic in Melbourne may never see the work being discussed in Sydney, Adelaide or Perth. That makes the idea of a single national theatre conversation difficult to sustain. It also makes reviewing expensive: someone has to travel, or publications need critics in several cities, for a production to be understood beyond the place where it was made.

For a period, the internet seemed to solve some of this. In the mid-2000s, Australian theatre blogs created a lively critical culture in which critics, artists and audiences regularly argued with one another in public. Much of that conversation centred on Melbourne and Alison Croggon's Theatre Notes, which ran from 2004 to 2012, but it extended well beyond it. Croggon eventually closed the blog for a very practical reason: serious criticism takes time, and she could no longer sustain that work alongside the writing that actually paid her.

RealTime gives us another version of this history. From 1994 to 2017 it created something Australia rarely has: sustained national coverage of experimental performance, dance, live art, sound and new media. At its print peak, 27,000 copies were distributed through around 1,000 locations nationally. Its archive now records more than two decades of work that might otherwise have left very little public trace. When regular publication stopped, the editors pointed partly to the loss of advertising revenue in the social media era.

This history matters because when criticism disappears, we lose more than opinions about whether a show was good or bad. We lose a record of artists developing over time, of small companies and experimental work, and of disagreements about what Australian theatre was doing at a particular moment.

Mainstream arts coverage has also become thinner. Specialist arts positions have repeatedly disappeared from Australian newsrooms, leaving fewer writers with the time and accumulated knowledge to follow an artist, company or artform over many years. When specialist positions disappear, arts coverage does not necessarily disappear altogether, but it can shift towards previews, interviews and event coverage rather than sustained criticism.

What has replaced that older structure is not one new model, but several overlapping ones.

Mainstream outlets, including The Age, The Australian, The Guardian Australia and the ABC, still give a production broad public visibility. But space is limited, and not every production will be reviewed.

Specialist arts publications, such as ArtsHub and Australian Arts Review, can cover more of the sector and bring more specialist knowledge to it. Their audiences are often smaller and more closely connected to the arts themselves.

Independent criticism can create room for longer or more experimental thinking, but the question of who pays for it never goes away. Later projects such as Witness Performance, founded in 2017 by Alison Croggon and Robert Reid, kept all their reviews free and refused advertising in order to stay independent, funding the work through Creative Victoria, the Australia Council and Monash University instead. Even then it did not last: when funding fell away in 2020 they had to drop their First Nations Emerging Critic program, and the site closed in 2021.

Peer-review platforms create another model. Theatre Travels now has a large national team, and says that most of its reviewers work in the arts themselves. It describes its reviews as deliberately colloquial and accessible, with the aim of encouraging people to see more theatre. That is worth noticing. A review written by another artist, partly to help build audiences for theatre, is operating under different conditions from a newspaper critic writing at editorial distance from the industry. Neither is automatically more or less valuable, but they are not doing exactly the same job.

Outside the major cities, the situation can be thinner again. In some regional communities, a small independent news outlet may be the only publication reviewing local theatre at all. That coverage can matter not only to audiences but also to artists trying to build a public record of their work, apply for funding or demonstrate that the work reached a community.

All of this makes Australian reviewing unusually interconnected. The person reviewing a production may also be an artist, academic, dramaturg, publicist or future collaborator. The publication may depend on subscriptions, government funding, industry support or unpaid labour. The company being reviewed may be part of the same small professional network.

That does not make independent criticism impossible. But it does mean that where a review appears, who is writing it, and how that writing is supported are part of the conditions in which criticism is produced.

Activity

Go back to one of the responses you collected to The Jungle and the Sea. What kind of critical environment does it come from? Who published it? Who wrote it? Who is the likely audience? And what might this particular outlet make easier, or harder, for that writer to say?

Section 8Your part in the critical conversation

Once criticism moves through digital platforms, participation is no longer something only reviewers do. Reading, sharing, liking, reposting, rating, commenting, screenshotting, and choosing not to respond all affect how a production circulates publicly.

That does not mean every response has to be serious or carefully argued. Criticism can be funny, angry, enthusiastic, playful or deeply personal. But it is worth thinking about two kinds of responsibility when you respond publicly to someone's work.

What you owe the work

Try to describe what happened before deciding what you think about it. Pay attention to performance, design, direction, dramaturgy and the choices the production makes. Separate "this is not something I like" from "this choice does not work", because those are different claims. Ask what the production seems to be trying to do, and then consider whether and how it achieves that.

What you owe the wider conversation

A public response does more than record your opinion. It can direct attention towards a work, shape how other people approach it, amplify another response, or turn disagreement into something much larger.

That does not mean avoiding criticism or softening a judgement you genuinely hold. It means giving the judgement enough context that someone else can understand how you arrived at it. If a directorial choice disappointed you, say what the choice was and what effect it had. If a performance moved you while others found it excessive, try to explain what you were responding to.

The aim is not to make criticism more polite. It is to make disagreement useful. A judgement becomes more interesting when a reader can see what you noticed, how you interpreted it, and why you reached the position you did.

A useful way to think about it is this: good criticism does more than tell us whether something was good or bad. It helps other people think more carefully about what the work did, how audiences responded to it, and why any of that might matter.
